'''Edwin Niblock Lightfoot, Jr.''' (September 25, 1925 – October 2, 2017)<ref>[http://www.cressfuneralservice.com/obituary/213102/Edwin-Lightfoot/ Edward N. Lightfoot Obituary]</ref> was an American [[chemical engineer]] and Hilldale Professor Emeritus in the department of chemical and biological engineering at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]]. He is known for his research in [[transport phenomena]], including biological mass-transfer processes, mass-transport reaction modeling, and separations processes.<ref name="uwm">{{cite web|url=http://www.engr.wisc.edu/che/faculty/lightfoot_edwin.html|title=Edwin N. Lightfoot|publisher=[[University of Wisconsin-Madison]]
|access-date=2009-11-15}}</ref> He, along with [[Robert Byron Bird|R. Byron Bird]] and Warren E. Stewart, co-authored the classic textbook ''[[Transport Phenomena (book)|Transport Phenomena]]''.<ref name="garfield">{{cite web|url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics1979/A1979HJ87300001.pdf|title=This Week's Citation Classic|date=1979-09-17|publisher=garfield.library.upenn.edu|access-date=2009-11-04|archive-date=September 20, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180920180945/http://www.garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics1979/A1979HJ87300001.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1974 Lightfoot wrote ''Transport Phenomena and Living Systems: Biomedical Aspects of Momentum and Mass Transport''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Lightfoot|first1=E. N.|title=Transport Phenomena and Living Systems: Biomedical Aspects of Momentum and Mass Transport|date=February 1974|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|location=New York|isbn=978-0471535157|pages=508|edition=1}}</ref> He was the recipient of the 2004 [[National Medal of Science]] in Engineering Sciences.<ref name="nsf">{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5100000000431|title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details|publisher=[[National Science Foundation]]|access-date=2009-11-15}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Lightfoot received his B.S. and Ph.D. degrees in [[chemical engineering]] from [[Cornell University]] in 1947 and 1950. After graduation he worked as a junior engineer at General Foods in Hoboken, New Jersey. His Ph.D. thesis (''Gasification of Coke)'' was supported by the Pittsburgh Consolidation Coal Company. After graduate school he worked for Pfizer & Co in Brooklyn where he received US Patent US2787578 A for his development of a commercial process for recovering and purifying vitamin B12.

He began his teaching career at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]] in 1953. There he co-authored ''[[Transport Phenomena (book)|Transport Phenomena]]'' with his colleagues R. Byron Bird and Warren E. Stewart. This first edition of this book was in print for 41 years and was translated into five languages. A second edition followed in 2001. In 1974, Lightfoot wrote ''Transport Phenomena and Living Systems: Biomedical Aspects of Momentum and Mass Transport''.

Lightfoot was the Hilldale Professor of Chemical Engineering, and upon his retirement in 1996, Hilldale Professor Emeritus in the department of chemical and biological engineering, as the department was renamed. His research interests were in the development of improved separation processes and controlling the dynamics of biological systems. In later life, he turned his attention to ways of developing scientifically informed intuition in bioengineers (in particular [[quantum biology]]).

Lightfoot was an inventor, holding US patents US2996430A for synthetic ion exchange resin recovery of vitamin b12 (Pfizer), US3094936A for fuel cell for sump pumps (A. O. Smith), US7141171 for membrane cascade-based separation<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.warf.org/documents/ipstatus/P04423US.PDF |title=US7141171 for membrane cascade-based separation |access-date=October 21, 2017 |archive-date=March 9, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190309190920/https://www.warf.org/documents/ipstatus/P04423US.PDF |url-status=dead }}</ref> (2006), and an additional patent with Michael Cochrem for membrane cascade-based separation,<ref>[https://www.warf.org/technologies/research-tools/synthesis-purification/summary/membrane-cascade-based-separation-p06389us.cmsx membrane cascade-based separation]</ref> a counter flow cascade system that features a novel separation technique.

==Awards and honors==
Lightfoot was a 2004 recipient of the [[National Medal of Science]], awarded by President [[George W. Bush]] "for his innovative research and leadership in transport phenomena focusing on biochemical and [[biomedical engineering]] with application to blood oxygenation, bioseparation techniques, and diabetic responses."<ref name="nsf" />

As emeritus in 1996 Lightfoot received the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers|AICHE]] Keynote Speaker Award, for which he delivered the keynote speech at a convention in Chicago that year.<ref>{{cite web |title=Institute Lecturer Award - Award Winners |url=https://www.aiche.org/community/awards/institute-lecturer-award?page=3 |website=aiche dot org | date=March 28, 2012 |publisher=AICHE |access-date=14 September 2022}}</ref>

Lightfoot was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/peerCollaboration/profile.aspx?c=psa&q=lightfoot|title=Academy Member Connection|website=www.amacad.org|access-date=2017-10-09}}</ref> He was elected to the membership of both the [[National Academy of Engineering]] for "Contributions to mass transfer and separation processes, and research on quantitative design procedures in biochemical and biomedical engineering" in 1979<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nae.edu/28994.aspx|title=Dr. Edwin N. Lightfoot, Jr.|website=NAE Website|access-date=2017-10-08}}</ref> and the National Academy of Sciences in 1995. He was one of three members to be elected to both academies. He was a Founding Fellow of the American Institute of Medical and Biological Engineering (1992).

He was awarded the [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers|AIChE]]'s William Walker Award for contributions to chemical engineering literature (1985) and its Warren K. Lewis Award for Chemical Engineering Education (1991).

In 1985, he was awarded an honorary doctorate from the University of Trondheim (formerly Norwegian Institute of Technology and now the [[Norwegian University of Science and Technology]]), where he had worked on a Fulbright Research Scholarship in 1962.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ntnu.edu/phd/honorary-doctors|title=Honorary doctors|last=Fossen|first=Christian|website=www.ntnu.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-10-07}}</ref> In 2000, he was awarded an honorary doctorate from the [[Technical University of Denmark|Danish Technical University]] (DTU).<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.dtu.dk/english/Research/Research-at-DTU/Doctorates/Honorary-Doctorates|title=Honorary Doctorates - DTU|work=dtu.dk|access-date=2017-10-07|language=en}}</ref>

In the spring of 2016, the University of Wisconsin Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering hosted qbio 2016,<ref>[http://edlightfootsymp2016.che.wisc.edu/ qbio 2016]</ref> a symposium in honor of Lightfoot's 90th birthday.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.engr.wisc.edu/renowned-biochemical-engineer-edwin-n-lightfoot-passes-away/|title=Renowned biochemical engineer Edwin N. Lightfoot passes away - College of Engineering - University of Wisconsin-Madison|date=2017-10-07|work=College of Engineering - University of Wisconsin-Madison|access-date=2017-10-09|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Books==
Lightfoot is the co-author of several influential books in transport phenomena, including the classic textbook ''Transport Phenomena'', which was translated into many languages, including Spanish, Italian, Czech, Russian, and Chinese.

* ''Transport Phenomena''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bird |first1=R. Byron |last2=Stewart |first2=Warren E. |last3=Lightfoot |first3=Edwin N. |title=Transport Phenomena |date=2001 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-471-41077-2 |pages=912 |edition=2}}</ref>
* ''Transport Phenomena in Living Systems: Biomedical Aspects of Momentum and Mass Transport''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lightfoot |first1=Edwin |title=Transport phenomena and living systems |date=1973 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |location=New York |isbn=978-0471535157 |pages=495 |edition=1}}</ref>
